Body HTML:
There is no single "best" gas water heater. The best one for your home is the one that matches your venting, your gas supply, your hot water demand and the space you have. A top-rated model with the wrong vent type can cost more to install than the heater itself. This guide shows you how to compare gas tank water heaters on the specs that matter, in the order a plumber would check them.

1. Start with the vent type

Venting decides which models can go in your home without major changes. It is the first filter, before price or brand. Residential gas tanks use five main vent types:

Vent type How it works Best fit
Atmospheric Exhaust rises by natural draft through a draft hood into a B-vent or chimney. Direct replacement where an existing vertical flue is in good condition. No electricity needed for venting.
Powered damper Atmospheric venting with a damper that closes the flue between burner cycles. Same flue as atmospheric, with less standby heat loss up the chimney.
Power vent A blower pushes exhaust through plastic pipe, often out a side wall. No chimney nearby, or the flue is shared or unusable. Needs a 120V outlet.
Direct vent A sealed system that draws combustion air from outside and vents by natural draft through a wall. Tight spaces and closets, with no electricity needed for venting. Vent terminal location is limited.
Power direct vent A blower plus sealed combustion, with intake and exhaust both piped outside. Longer vent runs and sealed installations. Needs a 120V outlet.

If you are replacing an existing heater, the simplest path is almost always the same vent type you have now.

2. Match the fuel: natural gas or propane

Natural gas and propane models are built differently: the gas valve, orifice and burner are specific to the fuel. Buy the version that matches your supply. Some models can be field-converted with a manufacturer kit, but many cannot. Check the rating plate and model number. In Rheem's naming, an "N" usually means natural gas and a "P" means propane (for example, PROG50-36N and PROG50-36P).

3. Size by first-hour rating, not just gallons

The first-hour rating (FHR) is how much hot water the heater can deliver in one busy hour. It is printed on the EnergyGuide label. Two 50-gallon tanks can have different FHRs because their burners are different sizes. Add up your busiest hour (about 10 gallons per shower, plus any dishwasher or laundry), and choose a model whose FHR meets or slightly exceeds it. For help with the numbers, see What Size Water Heater Do I Need?

4. Compare BTU input and recovery

BTU/h input is the size of the burner. A higher input reheats water faster, which raises the first-hour rating without a bigger tank. As an example, residential 50-gallon gas models in our catalog range from about 33,000 BTU/h up to 100,000 BTU/h. Before choosing a high-input model, confirm with your installer that your gas line and meter can supply it.

5. Check efficiency (UEF)

Uniform Energy Factor (UEF) is the federal efficiency rating for water heaters. Higher is better. Compare UEF only between heaters in the same usage bin (low, medium or high), which is listed on the EnergyGuide label next to the rating. Standard atmospheric tanks sit at the low end of the range. Powered damper, power vent and condensing designs can rate higher. The label also shows an estimated yearly operating cost, which is a quick way to compare two models.

6. Look at features that matter over the long run

  • Warranty length. Tank and parts warranties vary by product line. For example, the Ruud Professional models we list carry an 8-year warranty. Read the manufacturer's terms; warranties usually require professional installation and proper maintenance.
  • Leak detection. Some lines include a leak sensor or automatic shutoff. Our water heater shut-off valves and leak protection can add this to any heater.
  • Installed top T&P valve. Some models ship with the relief valve on top, which can simplify replacing a heater that had its valve in that position.
  • Height. Short and tall versions of the same capacity help with low ceilings or narrow closets.
  • Low NOx. Some air districts, mainly in California, require ultra-low NOx burners. Check local rules before ordering.

7. Budget for the whole installation

The heater is only part of the job. You may also need a new gas flex connector, water connectors, a drain pan, an expansion tank, seismic straps or vent parts to meet current code. Plan for them together. See our water heater gas supplies and water heater connectors.

A quick comparison checklist

  1. Same vent type as the existing heater, or a planned vent change.
  2. Correct fuel: natural gas or propane.
  3. First-hour rating that meets your busiest hour.
  4. BTU input your gas line can supply.
  5. Best UEF you can afford within the right usage bin.
  6. Dimensions and clearances that fit the space.
  7. Warranty terms and the features you want.

Compare models side by side in our residential gas tank water heaters collection. It includes Rheem Professional Classic, Classic Plus and Prestige lines plus Ruud Professional models, in natural gas and propane.

Safety note: Installing a gas water heater involves gas piping, combustion air, venting and a T&P relief valve. Mistakes can cause gas leaks, carbon monoxide or scalding. Have a licensed plumber or gas fitter install it, and pull a permit where your local code requires one.

Frequently asked questions

What is the most important spec when comparing gas water heaters?

Vent type comes first, because it decides what can be installed without major work. After that, compare first-hour rating, BTU input and UEF.

Is a power vent water heater better than atmospheric?

Not by default. A power vent is useful when there is no usable chimney, or when you want to vent out a side wall. It needs electricity and has a blower that makes some noise. If your flue works, atmospheric or powered damper is often the simpler replacement.

Can I use a natural gas water heater with propane?

Only if the manufacturer offers an approved conversion kit for that exact model and it is installed by a qualified technician. Otherwise, buy the propane version.

Does a higher BTU water heater use more gas?

It burns gas faster while it is running, but it runs for a shorter time to heat the same water. Total gas use depends mostly on how much hot water you use and the heater's efficiency (UEF).

Navien and Rinnai are two of the most widely installed tankless water heater brands in North America, and both build reliable equipment. If you're replacing a tank or upgrading an older tankless unit, the "right" choice usually depends less on the logo and more on your installation: your venting route, whether you need recirculation, your gas supply, and which brand local installers know best.

This guide compares the two brands on the points that matter: condensing vs non-condensing lines, efficiency (UEF), venting, recirculation and published warranty terms. We sell Navien, and we say so up front. We've kept this comparison to facts each manufacturer publishes, so you can make your own call.

Quick overview of each brand's lineup

Navien

  • NPE-2 series (condensing): Navien's main residential condensing line, sold in two versions.
    • NPE-S2 (standard): Rated at 0.96 UEF.
    • NPE-A2 (ComfortFlow): Adds a built-in buffer tank and recirculation pump. Rated at 0.95 UEF.
    Both use dual stainless steel heat exchangers and are sold in sizes up to 199,900 BTU/h.
  • NHW series (non-condensing): A compact line with a stainless steel heat exchanger. Navien lists 0.81 UEF across the NHW models. It comes as the NHW-SU (indoor/outdoor) and the NHW-AI (indoor, with a built-in recirculation pump and buffer tank).

Rinnai

  • SENSEI RX series (condensing): Rinnai's residential condensing line. Rinnai lists up to 0.98 UEF on select RX models. Models with a "P" in the name (such as the RXP) include a built-in recirculation pump.
  • RE series (non-condensing): Rinnai's current non-condensing residential line. Pump-equipped REP models offer Rinnai's Smart-Circ recirculation, which learns your household's hot water routine.

Both brands also sell commercial and boiler-combi products, which are beyond the scope of this guide.

Condensing vs non-condensing: the biggest decision

Before you choose a brand, decide whether you want a condensing or a non-condensing unit. This choice affects price, venting and efficiency more than brand does.

Condensing (Navien NPE-2, Rinnai SENSEI RX) Non-condensing (Navien NHW, Rinnai RE)
Efficiency Higher: roughly 0.95 – 0.98 UEF Lower: about 0.81 UEF on the models cited above
Venting Plastic vent pipe (PVC/CPVC/polypropylene), as allowed by the manual Brand-specific concentric vent or stainless steel vent
Condensate drain Required (a neutralizer is usually recommended) Not required
Up-front cost Higher Lower
Best for Long-term efficiency, flexible indoor venting Tight budgets, outdoor installs, simple replacements

If you're replacing an existing non-condensing unit and the vent is already in place, a like-for-like replacement is often the simplest job. If you're converting from a tank heater, a condensing unit with plastic venting can be easier to route through a sidewall.

Efficiency (UEF) compared

UEF (Uniform Energy Factor) is the Department of Energy rating for water heater efficiency. Higher is better. On condensing models, the two brands are close:

  • Navien NPE-S2: 0.96 UEF. NPE-A2: 0.95 UEF. Figures are from Navien's published specifications.
  • Rinnai SENSEI RX: Varies by model. Rinnai lists 0.98 UEF on its RX199iN, and some other RX models are rated around 0.96–0.97.

In practice, a few hundredths of a point in UEF makes a modest difference to your yearly energy bill. Correct sizing, gas supply and a good install usually matter more. Check the exact model's rating on the manufacturer's spec sheet or in the ENERGY STAR directory before you buy.

Venting

Venting is often the deciding factor because it drives installation cost.

  • Navien NPE-2: Navien lists 2" vent material with a maximum length of 75 feet, with length deductions for elbows. Approved materials include PVC Schedule 40, CPVC Schedule 80, approved polypropylene and stainless steel. Navien's installation manual covers other vent sizes and lengths. The ability to use 2" PVC is a big advantage when you replace an old tank heater and need to snake a new vent through tight framing.
  • Navien NHW-SU: Navien lists a 3" x 5" concentric vent system.
  • Rinnai SENSEI RX: Condensing, so it vents with plastic pipe as allowed by its installation manual. Check Rinnai's manual for the approved materials, diameters and maximum lengths for your model.
  • Rinnai RE/REP: Non-condensing models use a concentric vent system. Rinnai lists 3"/5" concentric venting for the REP models.

For a retrofit, ask your installer to price both brands with your actual vent route. The cheaper heater isn't always the cheaper install.

Recirculation: Navien ComfortFlow vs Rinnai recirculation

Recirculation keeps hot water close to your fixtures so you wait less at the tap. Both brands offer it built in, but they approach it a little differently.

Navien ComfortFlow (NPE-A2 and NHW-AI)

Navien's ComfortFlow models add a built-in recirculation pump and a small buffer tank. The buffer tank helps reduce the "cold water sandwich," a short burst of cold water you can get when a tankless unit restarts between uses. The unit's controls let you choose how and when recirculation runs. Navien's installation manual covers piping for homes with and without a dedicated hot water return line.

If you don't need recirculation, the standard Navien NPE-240S2 keeps things simple. If you do need it, the Navien NPE-240A2 with ComfortFlow builds it into the same footprint.

Rinnai recirculation (RXP and REP models)

Rinnai's pump-equipped models (the "P" versions) include a built-in recirculation pump. On the RE series, Rinnai's Smart-Circ feature learns your hot water usage over time and schedules recirculation around it, with no external controller needed. As with Navien, homes without a dedicated return line typically need a crossover valve accessory.

Both systems do the same core job. The difference is mostly in the buffer tank (a Navien ComfortFlow feature) and in each brand's scheduling and app approach.

Warranty terms as published

Warranty terms change, depend on the exact model and installation, and often require registration. Treat the figures below as a summary of what each brand publishes, and always read the current warranty document for your specific model.

  • Navien (NPE condensing series, residential): Navien's published warranty for standard or controlled recirculation installs is 15 years on the heat exchanger, 5 years on parts and 1 year on labor. Shorter terms apply to uncontrolled (continuous) recirculation installs.
  • Rinnai (SENSEI residential): Rinnai's published residential warranty is 15 years or 12,000 operating hours (whichever comes first) on the heat exchanger, and 5 years on other parts. Labor is covered for 5 years if the product is registered within 90 days of installation, otherwise 1 year.

Both brands require installation according to their instructions, and typically by a qualified professional. Improper installation, poor water quality, or missing descaling and maintenance can affect coverage.

Which should you buy?

Both brands make dependable tankless water heaters. Here's a practical way to decide:

  • Choose Navien NPE-2 if you want 2" PVC venting flexibility, a buffer tank with built-in recirculation (NPE-A2), or you're converting from a tank and need an easy vent route.
  • Choose Navien NHW if you want a compact non-condensing unit for a simpler or lower-cost install, including outdoor locations (NHW-SU).
  • Choose Rinnai if your installer is factory-trained on Rinnai, you're replacing an existing Rinnai and want to reuse the vent and connections, or a specific RX model fits your efficiency target.
  • Either way: Size the unit for your peak flow and winter temperature rise, confirm your gas line can supply the full BTU input, and use a licensed installer.

Ready to compare Navien models side by side? Browse our Navien tankless water heaters collection, with free shipping on qualifying orders. Not sure what size you need? Start with our tankless water heater sizing guide, or contact our team for help.

When a gas furnace won't heat, the problem is very often one of two small parts: the ignitor that lights the burners or the flame sensor that proves they're lit. Both are inexpensive and can be checked with basic tools. This guide covers how furnaces light, which part has failed, how to clean a flame sensor, how to test an ignitor, and how to choose a replacement, including Resideo (Honeywell) ignition modules.

How a modern gas furnace lights

Most modern furnaces light only when there's a call for heat, using one of three systems:

  • Hot surface ignition (HSI): the most common system in residential furnaces. A ceramic ignitor heats until it glows, then the control opens the gas valve and the burners light off the hot element.
  • Direct spark ignition (DSI): a high-voltage spark electrode lights the main burner directly. It's common on boilers, unit heaters and some furnaces.
  • Intermittent pilot (IP): a spark or hot surface lights a small pilot flame first. Once the pilot is proven, the main valve opens. This is common on older furnaces and many boilers.

Flame rectification: how the furnace knows it's lit

Every one of these systems needs proof of flame. A flame conducts a tiny electrical current, measured in millionths of an amp (microamps), and it conducts it better in one direction than the other. The control sends a voltage to the flame sensor rod, and the burner ground completes the circuit through the flame. If the control doesn't see that rectified current within a few seconds of opening the gas valve, it shuts the gas off.

Some systems use a separate flame rod (remote sense). Others use the same electrode to ignite and to sense (local sense or single-rod). This matters when you choose replacement parts.

Symptoms: is it the ignitor or the flame sensor?

Watch a heating cycle through the sight glass or with the burner door off. A typical HSI sequence is: inducer fan starts, pressure switch closes, ignitor glows, gas valve opens, burners light.

  • Burners light, then shut off after a few seconds: the classic dirty flame sensor symptom. The flame is there, but the control can't prove it. After several retries, many controls go into lockout.
  • No glow at all: the ignitor may be cracked or burned open. It could also mean the control isn't sending power to it, so test before you buy.
  • Ignitor glows, but burners never light: look at gas supply, the gas valve or the control, not the ignitor. Check that the gas is on at the appliance shut-off.
  • Spark but no light (DSI or pilot systems): check the electrode gap, the ignition cable and the ground connection.

Most furnace controls have a status LED that blinks a fault code. Compare the blink pattern with the chart on the inside of the furnace door before replacing anything.

Safety first

  • Turn off the power at the furnace service switch or the breaker. The ignitor runs on line voltage in most HSI furnaces, usually 120 VAC.
  • Turn off the gas at the manual shut-off valve on the furnace supply line.
  • Let the burner area cool for several minutes.
  • If you smell gas, don't touch any switches. Leave the building and call your gas utility from outside.
  • Take a photo of the wiring before you disconnect anything.
  • Follow your furnace manufacturer's instructions. If you're not comfortable with any step, call a licensed HVAC technician.

Where is the flame sensor on a furnace?

Remove the upper and lower furnace doors and find the burner assembly. The flame sensor is a thin, straight or bent metal rod set in a white porcelain insulator, mounted on a bracket so the tip sits in the burner flame. It's held in place by a single screw (often a 1/4-inch hex head) and has one wire attached. On many furnaces it sits at the far end of the burner row from the ignitor, so it only sees flame after the fire has carried across every burner.

How to clean a furnace flame sensor

  1. Turn off the power and gas, and let the burners cool.
  2. Disconnect the single wire from the sensor terminal.
  3. Remove the mounting screw and slide the sensor straight out. Handle it gently, because the porcelain can crack.
  4. Lightly rub the metal rod with a fine non-woven abrasive pad or very fine steel wool until the dull film is gone. You're removing oxide, not metal.
  5. Don't use coarse sandpaper or emery cloth. It leaves deep scratches that collect deposits faster, and it can leave grit on the rod.
  6. Wipe the rod with a clean, dry paper towel.
  7. Check the porcelain for cracks and the rod for heavy pitting or warping. If you see either, replace the sensor.
  8. Reinstall it in the same position, reconnect the wire, and make sure the burner assembly is properly grounded.
  9. Restore gas and power and run a full heating cycle. The burners should stay lit.

If the furnace still shuts down after a few seconds, check the ground wire, the burner flame (it should be mostly blue and touch the rod), and the sensor position. A sensor that fouls quickly can point to a combustion problem that needs a professional.

How to test a furnace ignitor

Visual check

With the power off, remove the ignitor (usually one or two screws and a plug). Never touch the element itself. Hold it by the ceramic base. Look for hairline cracks, white or chalky spots, and broken or burned leads. A cracked ignitor should be replaced even if it still glows.

Resistance (ohms) test

  1. Unplug the ignitor from the wiring harness.
  2. Set a multimeter to ohms and touch the probes to the two ignitor pins.
  3. An open circuit (OL or infinite) means the element is broken and must be replaced.
  4. A reading means the element is continuous. Compare it with the manufacturer's spec for that ignitor. Many 120 V silicon carbide ignitors read in the tens of ohms at room temperature, but ranges vary by model and material, so use the published figure rather than a general rule.

If the ignitor tests good but never glows, the control may not be sending voltage. Testing live 120 V circuits is a job for a qualified technician.

Furnace ignitor replacement: choosing the right part

Match the OEM part number first

The surest fit is the exact part listed in your furnace's parts list, or a direct replacement for it. Read the part number off the old ignitor or the furnace's rating plate. Ignitors that look alike can differ in voltage, lead length, connector and bracket. Our Resideo Q4100C9040/U silicon carbide hot surface ignitor is one example of an OEM-style replacement with a specific lead length and connector.

Universal ignitor kits

If you can't source the original, a universal kit with adapter brackets is a practical option. Check the kit's cross-reference before you buy:

  • Resideo Q3200U1004/U Glowfly multisystem 120 VAC hot surface ignitor
  • Resideo Q3205U1107/U universal silicon nitride ignitor with adapter brackets. Resideo lists it for remote flame sense applications only, so it's not for single-rod (local sense) systems.
  • DiversiTech IG1100 universal round silicon carbide ignitor kit, 120 V with three brackets

Silicon carbide vs silicon nitride

  • Silicon carbide: the traditional grey element. It works well but is brittle and sensitive to handling.
  • Silicon nitride: a newer, tougher element that's generally more resistant to breakage and heats up quickly.

Either can be the right choice, as long as the voltage, mounting and sensing type match your appliance. Never put a lower-voltage ignitor on a 120 V circuit, or the reverse.

Ignition control modules for furnaces and boilers

The ignition module runs the light-off sequence and holds the safety logic. If the ignitor and sensor test good but the appliance won't light, suspect the module. Common Resideo (Honeywell) families include:

  • S8610U intermittent pilot control: the S8610U3009/U is a universal intermittent pilot module with continuous retry for natural or LP gas. It's also part of the Y8610U6006/U kit with a VR8304M gas valve.
  • S8910U hot surface ignition module: the S8910U3000/U is a universal module for 120 V hot surface ignition with single or dual rod flame sensing, with timings set on the module.
  • S8701 and S8801 direct spark modules: 24 VAC DSI controls for furnaces, boilers and heating appliances. The S8701 has an internal spark generator, while the S8801 uses an external one. Versions differ by rod count (1-rod or 2-rod), trial-for-ignition time (4, 6, 11 or 21 seconds) and alarm terminal. Examples: S8701A1114/U and S8801A1110/U.

Match the trial-for-ignition time, rod configuration and prepurge exactly. The trial time is a safety rating set by the appliance manufacturer, not a preference. Never substitute a module with a longer trial time than the original.

/U vs /B part numbers: some Resideo modules come in two versions. The /U suffix is individually boxed and the /B suffix is a bulk pack. The part and specifications are the same; only the packaging differs. For example, S8701A1114/B and S8801A1110/B are the bulk-pack versions of the modules above.

On intermittent pilot systems with a SmartValve and hot surface pilot, the combined ignitor and flame rod can be replaced as one piece, such as the Resideo Q3400A1016/U 24-inch igniter/flame rod assembly.

When to call a pro

  • You smell gas, or you see soot, scorching or flame rolling out of the burner area.
  • A new sensor or ignitor doesn't fix the problem.
  • The ignitor keeps failing after short service lives, which can point to voltage or control problems.
  • The job involves replacing a gas valve or ignition module, checking gas pressure or measuring flame current.

Shop the parts

  • Gas ignition components: ignitors, flame sensors, ignition modules and cables
  • Pilot, burner and ignition parts
  • Resideo Q354A1018/U flame sensor, 6.37 in rod height
  • DiversiTech PFS010 flame sensor (replaces Goodman 013F00010, 20488501, B1172606)
  • Resideo Q3205U1107/U universal silicon nitride ignitor
  • Resideo S8910U3000/U universal hot surface ignition module
  • Resideo S8610U3009/U intermittent pilot ignition control

Replacing the thermostat too? See our thermostat wiring guide for beginners.

Frequently asked questions

How often should I clean my furnace flame sensor?

Many technicians check and clean it during annual furnace maintenance. If it fouls again within weeks, have the combustion and air supply checked.

Can I clean a flame sensor with sandpaper?

It's best not to. Coarse sandpaper scratches the rod and can leave grit behind. Use a fine non-woven abrasive pad or very fine steel wool, then wipe it clean.

How long does a furnace ignitor last?

It varies with type, cycling and handling. Silicon nitride ignitors are generally more durable than silicon carbide. Touching the element during service is a common cause of early failure.

Why does my furnace light and then shut off?

Most often it's a dirty or poorly grounded flame sensor. Other causes include a weak flame, a cracked sensor insulator, reversed polarity on the 120 V supply, or a failing control.

Need help matching a part? Send us the model number from your furnace or boiler and the number printed on the old ignitor, sensor or module, and we'll help you find the right replacement.

When a furnace runs its blower and tries to light but the burners never come on, the gas valve gets blamed fast. Sometimes it really is the valve. More often it is the igniter, the flame sensor, a pressure switch or the thermostat. This guide explains what a furnace gas valve does, how to tell whether yours has failed, and how to read the label so you can pick the right Honeywell (now Resideo) replacement, from the common VR8205 to universal and two-stage models.

Safety first: a gas valve controls fuel to a burner. A wrong part, a loose fitting or an incorrect pressure setting can cause a fire, an explosion or carbon monoxide. Replacing and adjusting a gas valve is work for a qualified, licensed technician in most areas, and many jurisdictions require a permit. Use this guide to understand the job and choose the right part, then follow the appliance manufacturer's instructions and your local code.

What does a furnace gas valve do?

A modern furnace gas valve is a combination gas control. In one body it combines:

  • A manual shutoff: the ON/OFF knob or switch on top of the valve.
  • Redundant automatic valves: two valve seats in series, opened by 24-volt coils only when the ignition control says it is safe.
  • A pressure regulator: it holds the outlet (manifold) pressure steady even as the supply pressure changes. A common natural gas setting is 3.5 inches of water column (in WC), but the correct value is always the one on the appliance rating plate.

The valve does not decide when to fire. The thermostat calls for heat, the furnace control runs the inducer and proves the pressure switch, the igniter or pilot lights, and only then does the control send 24 volts to the valve. If the flame is not proved, the control closes the valve again.

Signs of a bad furnace gas valve

Before you buy a valve, rule out the parts that fail more often. Work through the sequence in order:

  1. Thermostat and power. Is the thermostat calling for heat, is the furnace switch on and is the door switch closed? A thermostat with a blank screen or a missing C-wire can look like a furnace problem.
  2. Error code. Count the LED flashes on the furnace control board and look them up on the chart inside the door.
  3. Ignition. Does the hot surface igniter glow or the spark ignitor click? If nothing lights, see our guide to testing a furnace ignitor and flame sensor.
  4. Flame that drops out. If burners light for a few seconds and then shut off, a dirty flame sensor is the usual cause, not the valve.

The gas valve becomes the suspect when the furnace reaches the ignition step, the igniter is hot or sparking, 24 volts AC is present at the valve terminals during that trial, the manual knob is ON, gas is available at the inlet, and still no gas flows to the burners. Other signs include a valve that hums but will not open, a burner that will not shut off when the call ends (shut the gas off and call a technician right away) or a regulator that will not hold the rated manifold pressure. A technician confirms this with a meter and a manometer.

How to choose the right replacement gas valve

The fastest way to an exact match is the label on the old valve. Write down the full model number (for example VR8205A2024) and compare five things.

1. Ignition type

The ignition system on the furnace decides the valve family. In the Honeywell/Resideo VR series:

Ignition system How it lights Common valve families
Standing pilot A pilot burns all the time and a thermocouple proves it VR8200, VR8300 (24V); VR4300 (120V)
Intermittent pilot A spark lights a pilot on each call, then the main burner opens VR8204, VR8304
Direct ignition A hot surface igniter or spark lights the main burner directly VR8205, VR8215, VR8305
Universal Built to serve intermittent pilot and direct ignition systems VR8245, VR8345

Examples in stock include the Resideo VR8205A2024, the VR8304M4507 intermittent pilot valve and the VR8300A4516 standing pilot valve. Resideo's SmartValve models, such as the SV9510M2511, combine the gas valve with ignition control in one unit and are matched to specific appliances, so replace one with the same SmartValve type.

2. Single-stage or two-stage

Two-stage furnaces need a two-stage valve with two outlet pressures, such as the VR8205Q2555, set at 1.7/3.5 in WC, or the VR8305Q4500 with 3/4 inch connections. A single-stage valve on a two-stage furnace will not give you low fire, and a two-stage valve on a single-stage furnace needs the wiring and settings the appliance maker specifies.

3. Opening characteristic

The letter after the family number often reflects how the valve opens. Standard opening valves open fully at once. Slow opening valves (such as the VR8205H1003) ramp up gradually for a softer light-off. Step opening valves (such as the VR8205C1024) open to a low step first, then to full rate. Replace like with like unless the furnace manufacturer approves a different type, because the opening characteristic affects smooth, quiet ignition.

4. Pipe size and orientation

Residential valves are usually 1/2 inch x 1/2 inch or 3/4 inch x 3/4 inch NPT, with some 1/2 x 3/4 inch models such as the VR8305M3506. Check whether your outlet is straight or angled. Resideo sells replacement 1/2 inch angle flanges and 3/4 inch angle flanges with hex screws, plus 3/4 x 1/2 inch reducer bushings.

5. Gas type, pressure and voltage

Valves ship set for natural gas or LP, and some include a conversion kit. For single-stage VR82xx/VR83xx valves with standard or slow opening regulators, use the 393691 natural-to-LP kit or the 394588 LP-to-natural kit; these kits are not for step-opening valves. Two-stage valves use their own kits, such as the 396021 two-stage natural-to-LP kit. Finally, confirm the coil voltage: most furnaces use 24 volts AC, while 120-volt valves like the VR4300 are a different design.

Honeywell or Resideo: is it the same valve?

Resideo now makes and supports the residential gas controls that were sold under the Honeywell name, and it uses the same model numbers. A part ending in /U is a trade-packaged replacement version of that valve. If your old label says Honeywell VR8205A2024, the Resideo VR8205A2024/U is the matching replacement.

Can a universal valve replace my old one?

Often, yes. Universal valves such as the VR8345M4302, the VR8345Q4563 and the 1/2 inch VR8245M2530 are designed to cover intermittent pilot and direct ignition appliances, which is why service technicians keep them on the truck. Before you substitute, confirm that the replacement matches your pipe size, stage count, opening characteristic, gas type and capacity, and that the furnace manufacturer allows it. When the ignition module is the failed part instead, a universal module such as the Resideo S8610U3009 can replace many intermittent pilot controls.

How a gas valve is replaced (overview)

This overview is so you know what a correct job looks like. It is not a substitute for the manufacturer's instructions.

  1. Shut off gas and power. Close the manual gas cock ahead of the furnace and switch off the furnace power.
  2. Label the wires and take photos of the valve, wiring and pilot tubing.
  3. Remove the valve from the gas line and manifold. Support the piping so you don't strain other joints.
  4. Install the new valve with the flow arrow pointing toward the burners, using new flanges or fittings as needed and a thread sealant rated for gas. Do not put sealant on the first threads, where it could enter the valve.
  5. Convert for LP if needed, using the correct kit.
  6. Leak test. Turn the gas back on and check every joint with a gas leak detection solution. Never use a flame.
  7. Set and verify pressure. With a manometer, check inlet and manifold pressure against the rating plate and adjust only within the valve's range.
  8. Run several full cycles and watch for smooth ignition, a steady flame and a clean shutdown.

If you smell gas at any point, leave the building and call your gas utility from outside.

Water heater and boiler gas valves

Tank water heaters use a different kind of gas control with a built-in thermostat, such as the Resideo WT8840C1000 (a trade replacement for many Rheem atmospheric heaters). For pilot problems on those, see our water heater thermocouple guide. Many boilers use the same VR-series valves as furnaces, so the same selection steps apply.

  • Direct ignition: VR8205A2024, VR8215S1248T, VR8215S1503, VR8205Q2555 (two-stage)
  • Intermittent pilot and standing pilot: VR8204M1091, VR8304M4507, VR8200A2124, VR8300A3518 kit with thermocouple
  • Universal: VR8345M4302, VR8245M2530
  • Kits and controls: 393691 LP kit, 394588 natural gas kit, S8610U3009 ignition control

Browse all gas valves, gas ignition components, thermocouples or everything from Resideo.

Frequently asked questions

How do I know if my furnace gas valve is bad?

If the igniter works, the valve gets 24 volts during the ignition trial and gas is available at the inlet, but no gas reaches the burners, the valve is likely at fault. A technician confirms it with a meter and a manometer.

Is the VR8205 a universal gas valve?

No. The VR8205 family is for direct ignition (hot surface or direct spark) appliances. Universal models are the VR8245 and VR8345 families.

Can I replace a Honeywell gas valve with a Resideo valve?

Yes, when the model number matches. Resideo makes the Honeywell-branded residential gas controls and uses the same model numbers, often with a /U suffix.

Can I install a furnace gas valve myself?

Many areas require a licensed technician or a permit for gas work. Even where it is allowed, the job needs a leak test and a manometer pressure check, so most homeowners hire a pro.

Note: This guide is general information. Always follow the appliance manufacturer's instructions and local codes for gas appliance service.

A blank Honeywell thermostat screen almost always means one thing: the thermostat has lost power. The good news is that the cause is usually simple, such as dead batteries, a tripped breaker, a furnace door that isn't fully closed, or a blown fuse on the furnace control board. This guide walks through each cause in order, from the easiest fix to the ones that need a multimeter. It covers Honeywell Home thermostats made by Resideo, including the PRO series, FocusPRO and T-series models, and explains when it's time to replace the thermostat.

First: how is your thermostat powered?

Honeywell thermostats get their power in one of three ways, and knowing which one you have tells you where to look.

  • Batteries only. Many basic non-programmable and programmable models run on AA or AAA batteries, using the thermostat wires only to switch the system on and off.
  • Batteries or hardwired. Many PRO, FocusPRO and T-series models can run on batteries or on 24 VAC from the HVAC system through a common wire (C-wire). For example, the FocusPRO 100 TH1110U4000/U lists both battery (2 AA) and hardwired power. When a C-wire is connected, the batteries may act as a backup.
  • Hardwired only (C-wire required). Wi-Fi models such as the FocusPRO Wi-Fi TH2110WF4008/U and the T6 Pro Smart TH6220WF2006/U need continuous 24 VAC power. If that power stops, the screen goes blank.

If you're not sure, gently pull the thermostat straight off its wallplate. Look for a battery compartment on the back and check whether a wire is connected to the terminal marked C.

Safety first

  • Thermostat wiring is low voltage (24 VAC), but the furnace or air handler runs on 120 VAC or higher. Turn off power at the furnace service switch or breaker before opening the equipment or touching the control board.
  • Take a photo of the thermostat and control board wiring before you disconnect anything.
  • Don't bypass safety switches, such as the door switch or a condensate float switch, to get the system running.
  • If you smell gas, leave the building and call your gas utility from outside.
  • If you're not comfortable with any step, call a licensed HVAC technician.

Step 1: Replace the batteries

This fixes more blank screens than anything else. Even a hardwired thermostat may go blank or act up if it's set up to run on batteries and they're dead.

  1. Pull the thermostat off the wallplate, or open the battery door if your model has one.
  2. Replace all batteries with fresh alkaline batteries of the size shown in the compartment. Don't mix old and new batteries.
  3. Check the polarity (+ and -) markings and that the battery contacts are clean and not corroded.
  4. Snap the thermostat firmly back onto the wallplate. Wait a minute for the display to come on.

Many Honeywell models show a low-battery warning before the batteries die, so a blank screen with no warning beforehand points more toward a power problem at the HVAC equipment.

Step 2: Check the breaker and furnace switch

On hardwired thermostats, the 24 VAC power comes from a transformer inside the furnace or air handler. If the equipment has no power, neither does the thermostat.

  • Check the breaker for the furnace or air handler at your main electrical panel. Reset it if it has tripped. If it trips again, stop and call a technician.
  • Find the service switch near the furnace. It often looks like a light switch on the wall or the side of the unit, and it's easy to turn off by accident.
  • On some systems the air handler for a heat pump or AC has its own breaker, separate from the outdoor unit.

Step 3: Make sure the furnace door is closed

Most furnaces and many air handlers have a door safety switch, a small push-button switch that cuts power to the unit when the blower door is removed. If the door was taken off to change a filter and wasn't put back tightly, the switch stays open, the furnace has no power, and a hardwired thermostat goes blank. Reseat the door so it presses the switch fully, then check the screen.

Step 4: Check the fuse on the furnace control board

Many furnace and air handler control boards have a small automotive-style blade fuse, commonly rated 3 or 5 amps, that protects the 24 VAC thermostat circuit. If two thermostat wires touched each other, such as during a thermostat installation, or a wire shorted against metal, this fuse blows and the thermostat loses power.

  1. Turn off power to the furnace at the service switch or breaker.
  2. Remove the furnace door and find the control board. The fuse is usually plugged into the board and labeled.
  3. Pull the fuse and look at the metal strip inside. A broken strip or a darkened fuse means it has blown.
  4. Replace it only with a fuse of the same amp rating marked on the board. Never use a larger fuse.
  5. Before restoring power, look for the cause: a bare wire touching metal, a pinched thermostat cable, or loose strands at the thermostat or the outdoor unit. A new fuse will blow again if the short is still there.

Many control boards also have a status LED. If it's off with power on and the fuse is good, the board may not be getting power, or the transformer may have failed.

Step 5: Check the condensate float switch

Air conditioners, heat pumps and high-efficiency furnaces produce condensate water. To prevent overflow damage, many systems have a float switch in the drain line, drain pan or condensate pump. When water backs up, the switch shuts the system off.

Depending on how it's wired, a float switch may break the cooling call only, or it may break the 24 VAC power (R) wire. If it's wired into the power circuit, a full drain pan or clogged drain line can turn a hardwired thermostat's screen blank. Look for standing water in the pan under the air handler or a float switch that's tripped. Clear the drain line, empty the pan, and let the switch reset. If the drain keeps clogging, have the drain system checked.

Step 6: Check for loose or broken wiring

  • At the thermostat, make sure each wire is tight under its terminal and that no bare copper touches another terminal.
  • Check that the thermostat is fully seated on the wallplate. A thermostat that isn't snapped all the way on won't make contact with the terminals.
  • At the furnace control board, check that the R and C wires (and any others) are tight.
  • If you have a multimeter, set it to AC volts and measure between R and C at the thermostat wallplate. You should see roughly 24 to 28 VAC. No voltage means the problem is upstream at the furnace, the wiring or the transformer.

If your Wi-Fi thermostat has no C-wire at all, you'll need to add one. Our thermostat C-wire guide explains your options, including a spare wire in the cable, new thermostat wire, or a C-wire adapter such as the Honeywell Home THP9045A1023/U WireSaver, which installs at the equipment and lets an existing four-wire cable do the job of a five-wire one.

Step 7: Reset the thermostat

If power has been restored but the screen is still blank, frozen or showing nonsense, a reset can clear it. Start with a simple restart:

  1. Pull the thermostat off the wallplate (or turn off the HVAC breaker for a hardwired model).
  2. Remove the batteries, if any.
  3. Wait about a minute.
  4. Reinstall the batteries, snap the thermostat back on, and restore power.

Steps beyond a restart vary by model:

  • PRO 1000, PRO 2000 and PRO 3000: a power cycle like the one above is usually all that's needed. Programmable models may need the time and schedule checked afterward.
  • FocusPRO models: after a restart, check the clock, schedule and installer settings. Installer settings such as system type and heat pump setup live in the installer menu, which is described in the installation manual.
  • T-series (T4 Pro, T6 Pro and T6 Pro Smart): these have reset options in the menu, including schedule, Wi-Fi and factory resets on Wi-Fi models.

A factory reset can erase installer settings, so photograph them first. For step-by-step help, see our guide on how to reset a Honeywell thermostat.

When to replace the thermostat

Replace the thermostat if it has confirmed power (fresh batteries and about 24 VAC between R and C) but the screen stays blank after a reset. Other reasons to replace it include a cracked display, water damage, corrosion inside, or an older model you want to upgrade. Match the replacement to your system: the number of heating and cooling stages, conventional or heat pump, and whether you have a C-wire.

Popular Resideo / Honeywell Home replacements

  • PRO 3000 TH3110D1008/U: a non-programmable digital thermostat with a backlit display, for 1 heat/1 cool conventional systems or single-stage heat pumps with no auxiliary heat.
  • PRO 1000 TH1110DV1009/U: a simple, single-stage non-programmable model in a vertical case.
  • FocusPRO 100 TH1110U4000/U: non-programmable, 1 heat/1 cool, battery or hardwired.
  • FocusPRO 200 TH2110U4004/U: programmable (7-day, 5-1-1 or 5-2), 1 heat/1 cool, battery or hardwired.
  • T6 Pro TH6210U2001/U: programmable, up to 2 heat/1 cool.
  • FocusPRO Wi-Fi TH2110WF4008/U and T6 Pro Smart TH6220WF2006/U: Wi-Fi models for app control. Both need a C-wire.

Installing it yourself? Follow our thermostat wiring guide for beginners.

Shop the parts

  • Honeywell PRO series thermostats
  • Non-programmable thermostats
  • Programmable thermostats
  • Smart thermostats
  • Thermostat accessories, including C-wire adapters and cover plates
  • Thermostat wire

Frequently asked questions

Why is my Honeywell thermostat blank after changing the batteries?

Check that the batteries are fresh, the right size and installed with the correct polarity, and that the thermostat is fully snapped onto the wallplate. If it's a hardwired model, check the furnace breaker, service switch, door switch and control board fuse.

Why did my thermostat go blank after I replaced it?

The most common cause is a blown 3 or 5 amp fuse on the furnace control board, caused by wires touching during installation. A missing C-wire on a model that needs one is the other common cause.

Can a clogged AC drain make the thermostat screen go blank?

Yes, on systems where the condensate float switch interrupts the 24 VAC power wire. Clear the drain and the pan, and the switch should reset.

Does a blank screen mean the thermostat is broken?

Usually not. Most blank screens come from a power problem. Replace the thermostat only after you've confirmed it's getting power and a reset doesn't help.

Need help choosing a replacement? Send us the model number from the back of your thermostat and the wire letters on the wallplate, and we'll help you find a compatible Honeywell Home thermostat.

If you have a hot water boiler, there is a good chance a small gray box on the side of it decides when the burner fires and when the circulator runs. That box is the aquastat. When it fails or is set wrong, the boiler may not turn on, may short-cycle or may run too hot. This guide explains what an aquastat does, the main types (including the Honeywell/Resideo L4006, L8148 and L8124), how to read the settings, and how to choose a replacement.

Safety first: many aquastats and aquastat relays switch 120-volt power to the burner and circulator. Turn off the boiler's service switch and confirm the power is off before you open a cover. Boiler controls are safety devices; if you are not comfortable with line-voltage wiring, have a qualified heating technician do the work.

What is an aquastat?

An aquastat is a temperature-actuated switch for water. A sensing bulb sits in the boiler water, usually inside a brass or copper immersion well, and a switch inside the case opens or closes when the water reaches the set temperature. In a hot water heating system, aquastats do up to three jobs:

  • High limit: shuts the burner off when the boiler water reaches the maximum setting, so the boiler cannot overheat.
  • Low limit: keeps the boiler water at a minimum temperature, often to supply a tankless domestic hot water coil or to limit condensation in a cast iron boiler.
  • Circulator control: holds the circulator off until the water is hot enough, so cold water is not pushed into the system.

The differential is the temperature swing between the switch opening and closing. With a 180°F high limit and a 15°F differential, the burner shuts off at 180°F and is allowed to fire again near 165°F. A wider differential means longer, less frequent burns; a narrow one holds temperature more tightly.

Types of aquastats

Single-function immersion aquastats (L4006, L6006)

These are the simplest controls: one switch, one setting. Two terms matter when you read the label:

  • Breaks on rise means the switch opens as the temperature rises. That is how a high limit works, as on the L4006A1017 (100 to 240°F, adjustable 5 to 30°F differential).
  • Makes on rise means the switch closes as the temperature rises, the action used to start a circulator only once the water is hot, as on the L4006B1163.

Models with SPDT contacts, such as the L6006A1244, can be wired either way.

Manual reset high limits (L4006E, L4008E)

A manual reset aquastat is a backup safety limit. If the water ever reaches its setting, it locks out the burner and stays off until someone presses the reset button. Examples include the L4006E1000 (supplied with a 1/2 inch well) and the remote-bulb L4008E1156. A manual reset that keeps tripping is a warning sign: something is letting the boiler overheat, and the cause should be found before the boiler goes back into service.

Surface mount and remote bulb aquastats

Strap-on (surface mount) models, such as the L6006C1018, clamp to a pipe instead of using a well. Remote bulb models in the L4008 family have a capillary tube so the case can be mounted away from the sensing point.

Aquastat relays (L8148)

An aquastat relay combines a high limit with a relay that runs the burner and circulator from a low-voltage thermostat. The thermostat connects to the relay's T T terminals, and the control switches 120-volt power to the burner and pump. Resideo's L8148 relays, including the L8148A1017 (140 to 240°F, fixed 8°F differential) and the 180 to 240°F L8148E1265, are common on gas boilers. The L8148J1009 is a universal-mount version.

Triple aquastats (L8124)

A triple aquastat adds a low limit to the high limit and circulator functions. That is the classic control on oil boilers with a tankless coil, where the boiler stays warm all year to make domestic hot water. The L8124A1007 has a 130 to 240°F high limit with a fixed 10°F differential and a 110 to 220°F low limit with a 10 to 25°F adjustable differential. Multizone systems add a separate circulator and an R845A relay for each zone.

Electronic aquastats (L7224U)

The L7224U1002 universal electronic oil aquastat replaces the mechanical high limit and circulator controls on an oil-fired boiler with one electronic control. Instead of holding one high limit all winter, it can lower the boiler target when the heating load is light and raise it when the house calls hard. It uses a plug-in sensor, such as the 50001464-001 sensor assembly.

Boiler won't turn on? Check the aquastat

When a hot water boiler will not fire on the first cold night, the aquastat is one of the first places to look:

  1. Power and thermostat. Make sure the service switch is on, the fuse or breaker is good and the thermostat is calling for heat. A low-voltage thermostat on an aquastat relay connects to T T; jumping those terminals briefly is a common technician test.
  2. Manual reset. Look for a tripped reset button on any manual reset limit, and on the oil burner primary control. Press it once only. If it trips again, call a technician.
  3. Settings. Someone may have turned the high limit down. A setting below the water temperature keeps the burner off.
  4. Relay and transformer. On an L8148 or L8124, a failed transformer or relay can stop both the burner and the circulator.
  5. Not the aquastat? If the burner fires but the radiators stay cold, look at the circulator and air in the system. See how to choose a boiler circulator and how to bleed radiators and fix boiler pressure.

If your system has zone valves rather than zone pumps, also check the end switches; our guide to zone valve replacement covers them.

How to set a boiler aquastat

Always start with the boiler manufacturer's recommended settings. As general guidance:

  • High limit: set it high enough to heat the house on the coldest days but no higher than the boiler and system allow. Many baseboard systems run around 180°F; radiant floors run much cooler and usually need a mixing device. See our mixing valve guide.
  • Low limit: must be set below the high limit, with at least the gap the control's instructions call for. If you don't have a tankless coil, ask your technician whether the low limit can be turned down or off to save fuel, within the boiler maker's minimum water temperature.
  • Differential: a larger differential reduces short cycling; a smaller one gives steadier temperatures.

How to choose a replacement aquastat

Match the control coming out, not just the boiler nameplate. Check:

  1. Function: single limit, aquastat relay, triple aquastat or electronic.
  2. Switch action: breaks on rise, makes on rise or SPDT.
  3. Range and differential: for example 100 to 240°F with an adjustable differential, or a fixed differential.
  4. Reset type: automatic or manual reset.
  5. Mounting: immersion well, strap-on or remote bulb. If the old well is reused, check its thread size and insertion depth. Replacement wells include the 121371A (1/2 inch NPT) and 121371B (3/4 inch NPT).
  6. Voltage and wiring: 120V line voltage, 24V or millivolt thermostat circuits.

Coat the sensing bulb with heat conductive grease before sliding it into the well so it reads the water temperature accurately.

Shop the parts

  • Aquastat relays and triple aquastats: L8148A1017, L8148E1265, L8124A1007, L7224U1002
  • Limits and circulator controls: L4006A1017, L4006E1000 manual reset, L6006A1244, L4081B1047 dual control
  • Wells and accessories: 121371A well, 123869A well, heat conductive grease, R845A switching relay

Browse all aquastats and wells, circulator pumps or everything from Resideo.

Frequently asked questions

What does an aquastat do on a boiler?

It senses the boiler water temperature and switches the burner, the circulator or both, so the water stays within its working range and never exceeds the high limit.

What is the difference between an aquastat and a thermostat?

A room thermostat senses air temperature and calls for heat. An aquastat senses water temperature and decides whether the boiler can fire and the pump can run.

What should a boiler aquastat be set to?

Use the boiler manufacturer's settings. Many baseboard systems run a high limit around 180°F, with the low limit set lower by at least the gap the control requires.

Can I replace an L8148 with an L8124?

Not directly. They have different functions and wiring. Replace with the same type unless a technician confirms the system needs the extra low limit function.

Note: This guide is general information. Always follow the boiler and control manufacturer's instructions and your local code.

A combi boiler is one wall-hung appliance that does two jobs: it heats your home through radiators, baseboard or radiant floors, and it makes domestic hot water on demand for showers and taps, with no storage tank. Combis are popular in smaller homes and tight mechanical rooms, but they are not the right fit for every house. This guide explains how a combi works, how to size one, when a boiler plus an indirect tank is the better choice, and what venting, gas piping and maintenance involve.

What is a combi boiler?

"Combi" is short for combination boiler. Inside one cabinet you get a gas burner, a primary heat exchanger, a circulator, a diverter (3-way) valve, a small plate heat exchanger for domestic hot water and the controls that run it all. Most combis sold in the US today are condensing, high-efficiency units with sealed combustion.

A standard heating-only boiler, by contrast, makes hot water for the heating system only. If you also want stored hot water from it, you add a separate indirect water heater (an insulated tank with a coil that the boiler heats as its own zone).

How a combi heats your home and your water

A combi gives domestic hot water (DHW) priority. It switches between two modes:

  • Space heating mode. When a thermostat calls for heat, the burner fires and the internal pump circulates boiler water through the heating loop, just like a regular boiler. Modulating burners vary their output to match the load.
  • Hot water mode. When you open a hot tap, a flow sensor detects the draw. The diverter valve sends boiler water through the plate heat exchanger instead of the heating loop, and the burner ramps up to heat the cold water passing through the other side. Close the tap and the boiler returns to heating.

During a long shower the house gets no new heat, but a properly sized system rarely notices because radiators and floors hold heat. The domestic side works much like a gas tankless water heater. If you want the background on that, see how a tankless water heater works.

Combi boiler vs tankless water heater

People often compare a combi boiler to a tankless water heater because both make hot water on demand. The difference is what else they do:

Combi boiler Tankless water heater
Space heating Yes, through a hydronic system (radiators, baseboard, radiant) No (some can serve a fan coil or air handler with the right kit and approvals)
Domestic hot water On demand, with DHW priority On demand
Closed heating loop Yes: needs expansion tank, relief valve, fill valve and air removal No
Best for Homes with hydronic heat and moderate hot water demand Homes heated by a furnace or heat pump

If your house is heated by forced air, a tankless water heater is usually the simpler upgrade. If it has radiators or baseboard and an old boiler plus a tank-type water heater, a combi can replace both. For tankless sizing basics, read what size tankless water heater you need. For an explanation of condensing technology, which most combis use, see condensing vs non-condensing tankless water heaters.

How to size a combi boiler

A combi has two ratings, and you need to check both. Most sizing mistakes come from looking at only one.

1. Heating load (BTU/h)

The heating side should match the home's design heat loss, ideally from a room-by-room heat loss calculation (ACCA Manual J or a similar method). The nameplate on your old boiler is not a reliable guide, because many older boilers are oversized.

Turndown matters too. The Navien NCB-240/130H lists a heating input range of 13,000 to 130,000 BTU/h, and the IBC CX199 modulates from 20,000 to 199,000 BTU/h (10:1 turndown). A low minimum input lets the boiler run long, efficient cycles on mild days instead of short-cycling.

2. Hot water demand (GPM)

The domestic side is sized by flow rate in gallons per minute (GPM) at your temperature rise. Temperature rise is the difference between your incoming cold water and the hot water temperature you want, for example 50°F in, 120°F out = 70°F rise. A useful rule of thumb:

GPM ≈ BTU/h output ÷ (500 × temperature rise in °F)

A combi with about 190,000 BTU/h of DHW output at a 70°F rise gives roughly 5.4 GPM. That lines up with the NCB-240/130H, which lists 5.1 GPM at a 70°F rise from a 199,900 BTU/h DHW input. Add up the fixtures you will run at the same time (a showerhead is limited to 2.5 GPM by federal standards, and many use less) and compare. In cold-water regions your rise is larger, so the same unit delivers fewer GPM in winter.

Where the models fit

  • Smaller heat loads: Navien NCB-240/110H (110,000 BTU/h heating, 199,900 BTU/h DHW) and Lochinvar Noble NKC110N (110 MBH, 95% AFUE, natural gas).
  • Mid-size homes: Navien NCB-240/130H and IBC SFC160-1 (160,000 BTU/h input).
  • Larger heat loads: Navien NFC-250/175H and NFC-250/200H (210,000 BTU/h DHW input), IBC CX199, Noritz NRCB199DVNG and the US Boiler Alta ALTAC-200 (200,000 BTU/h input, pump included).

Always confirm the final choice with the manufacturer's sizing tables and your installer.

When a combi fits, and when to choose a boiler + indirect tank

A combi is usually a good fit when

  • The home has one to two (sometimes two and a half) bathrooms and rarely runs more than two hot fixtures at once.
  • Space is tight: a wall-hung combi frees the floor space of a boiler and a water heater.
  • The heat load is moderate and the house already has hydronic heat.
  • You want one appliance, one vent and one gas connection to service.

A boiler plus an indirect water heater is often better when

  • Several showers, a large soaking tub or a body-spray shower run at the same time. A tank stores a reserve that covers peaks a combi cannot.
  • Your incoming water is very cold or very hard. Hard water scales plate heat exchangers quickly.
  • The heat load is large, or you need many heating zones, and you would rather size the boiler to the heat loss alone.
  • You want hot water recirculation with minimal wait, which a storage tank handles more easily.

For the heating-only route, browse condensing boilers and pair one with an indirect water heater.

Combi boiler pros and cons

Pros: endless hot water within the unit's GPM limit, no standby tank losses, compact wall-hung design, high efficiency with modulation, and one appliance instead of two.

Cons: hot water flow is limited (a demanding household may notice), heating pauses while hot water runs, plate heat exchangers need descaling in hard water, and more components sit in one box, so a failure can take out both heat and hot water.

Venting a condensing combi (PVC, CPVC or polypropylene)

Condensing combis produce cool, acidic flue gas and condensate, so they vent through plastic or stainless pipe instead of a masonry chimney. Typical options are PVC, CPVC, polypropylene (PP) or stainless steel, as a two-pipe direct vent or a concentric kit. What is allowed depends on the model:

  • The Navien NCB-240/130H lists 2" or 3" venting in polypropylene, PVC, CPVC or stainless.
  • The IBC CX199 calls for 3" PVC, CPVC or PPs flue and intake, up to 150 ft equivalent length, and does not permit 2" PPs.

Maximum vent length shrinks with each elbow, and some manufacturers require CPVC or PP for the first section near the boiler. Follow the installation manual exactly, keep the terminals clear of windows, doors and snow lines, and run the condensate to a drain through a condensate neutralizer where required. See our polypropylene vent pipe for PP systems.

Gas line sizing: an important caveat

A combi can fire at around 200,000 BTU/h when making hot water. That is often more than double the old boiler or water heater it replaces, and the existing gas line may be too small. An undersized line can cause poor hot water performance, ignition faults and error codes.

  • A 3/4" gas connection on the appliance (as on the NCB-240/130H) does not mean a 3/4" line is enough. Pipe size depends on total connected load, pipe length and material, and your gas pressure.
  • Check the supply pressure range in the manual. The IBC CX199, for example, lists a 1/2" NPT gas inlet and 4 to 14 in. w.c. supply pressure.
  • Your gas meter and regulator must handle the added load.

Safety note: gas piping, venting and combustion setup should be done by a licensed installer following the manufacturer's manual, the fuel gas code and local requirements. A combustion analysis at startup is the only way to confirm safe, efficient operation.

Combi boiler maintenance

  • Check system pressure. The heating loop is a closed system. Look at the gauge or display when the system is cold and compare with the manual's range. Frequent pressure loss means a leak; rising pressure points to the expansion tank or fill valve. Our guide on how to bleed a radiator and fix high boiler pressure covers both.
  • Flush the DHW heat exchanger. In hard water areas, descale the plate heat exchanger on the schedule in the manual, using isolation valves and a pump-and-bucket flush kit as you would on a tankless heater. Tankless valve kits make this easier on the domestic side.
  • Clean the filters. Clean the cold water inlet filter and any heating return filter. A magnetic boiler filter such as the Navien NaviClean helps catch magnetite before it reaches the heat exchanger.
  • Inspect the condensate trap and vent. Make sure the trap is clean and full, and that the vent and intake terminals are clear.
  • Annual service. Have a professional inspect the burner, check combustion, test the relief valve and verify the expansion tank pre-charge once a year.
  • Learn the error codes. Navien owners can start with our Navien error codes guide. Many codes, such as ignition or flow faults, overlap with Navien combi models. Always confirm in your model's manual.

Shop the parts

  • Combination heating and DHW boilers
  • Navien combi boilers
  • Noritz combination boilers
  • Condensing boilers (heating only)
  • Indirect water heaters
  • Heating expansion tanks
  • Condensate neutralizers
  • Magnetic boiler filters

Frequently asked questions

What is a combi boiler in simple terms?

It is a boiler that heats your home and also heats your tap water instantly, without a storage tank. One appliance replaces a heating boiler and a water heater.

Is a combi boiler the same as a tankless water heater?

No. Both heat water on demand, but a combi also runs your hydronic heating system. A tankless water heater only makes domestic hot water.

Can a combi boiler run two showers at once?

Often yes, if the unit's GPM at your temperature rise covers both showerheads. With very cold incoming water or high-flow fixtures, a boiler with an indirect tank is the safer choice.

Do I need an expansion tank with a combi boiler?

The heating loop always needs expansion capacity. Some combis include an internal expansion vessel, others do not, and the built-in vessel may be too small for larger systems. Check the manual and size an external heating expansion tank if needed.

How long does a combi boiler last?

Lifespan depends on water quality, installation and maintenance. Annual service, clean system water and regular descaling in hard water areas make the biggest difference. Check the manufacturer's warranty terms for your model.

Every tank water heater collects sediment. Minerals in the water (mostly calcium and magnesium) settle to the bottom of the tank, along with sand and bits of a worn anode rod. Over time, that layer insulates the water from the gas burner, causes popping or rumbling noises, and can bury the lower element on an electric heater. Draining and flushing the tank once a year is one of the simplest maintenance jobs you can do to keep a water heater quiet, efficient and working longer.

This guide covers standard gas and electric tank water heaters. You'll need about an hour, a garden hose, and a few basic tools. Read the safety notes before you start, and always follow the instructions in your heater's manual if they differ from the general steps below.

When to flush (and when not to)

  • Once a year is a good general schedule. Homes with hard water may benefit from flushing every six months.
  • Signs you're overdue: popping, crackling or rumbling noises while the heater runs, hot water that runs out faster than it used to, or rusty or gritty water at the tap.
  • Use caution on an old tank that has never been flushed. On a heater that's 10+ years old with heavy buildup, sediment can clog the drain valve, and a corroded tank may start leaking once the sediment that was sealing a weak spot is disturbed. If your heater is near the end of its life, it may make more sense to plan a replacement.

What you'll need

  • A garden hose long enough to reach a floor drain, a laundry sink, or outside to a spot lower than the drain valve
  • A flat-head screwdriver or pliers (some drain valves have a slotted stem instead of a handle)
  • Work gloves and safety glasses
  • A non-contact voltage tester (electric heaters)

Safety first

The water in the tank is hot enough to scald. Water heaters are often set to 120°F or higher, and the water in the tank can be hotter than what reaches your faucets. Either let the tank cool for several hours (or overnight) after shutting it off, or work very carefully, wear gloves, and make sure the hose is secured where the water discharges.

  • Electric heaters: Turn the power off at the circuit breaker, not just at the thermostat. Electric water heaters typically run on 240 volts. Confirm the power is off with a voltage tester before you remove any access panels.
  • Gas heaters: If you smell gas at any point, stop, leave the area, and call your gas utility from outside. Don't operate switches or create sparks.
  • If you're not comfortable working with gas controls or 240-volt circuits, hire a licensed plumber.

Step 1: Turn off the gas or power

Gas water heater: Turn the gas control knob to Pilot or Off, as described on the label on your heater. Pilot keeps the pilot light lit while the main burner stays off, which makes restarting easier. If your heater has an electronic control or a power vent blower, also unplug it or switch off its power.

Electric water heater: Switch off the breaker that feeds the water heater. This step matters more than anything else in this guide, for reasons covered in Step 7.

Step 2: Shut off the cold water supply

Find the shut-off valve on the cold water inlet line, usually on the pipe that enters the top of the tank on the right side (often marked "cold"). Close it fully.

Step 3: Connect the hose and open a hot water faucet

  1. Thread a garden hose onto the drain valve near the bottom of the tank.
  2. Run the other end to a floor drain, a laundry sink, or outdoors. The end of the hose must be lower than the drain valve for the tank to drain by gravity.
  3. Open a hot water faucet somewhere in the house, ideally one on a floor above the heater. This lets air into the system so the tank drains freely instead of holding a vacuum.

Step 4: Drain the tank

Open the drain valve slowly. The water will be cloudy or discolored at first, and you may see sand-like particles. Draining a 40- or 50-gallon tank can take 20 minutes to an hour, depending on how much sediment is present and how freely the valve flows.

If the flow slows to a trickle while the tank is still full, sediment is probably clogging the valve. Closing the valve and opening it again, or briefly turning the cold supply on (Step 5), can help break up the clog. Don't force a stiff plastic drain valve, since many factory valves are plastic and can crack.

Step 5: Flush out the sediment

Once the tank is empty, or nearly empty:

  1. With the drain valve still open, open the cold water supply valve for a short burst of 30 seconds to a minute. The incoming water stirs up sediment on the bottom of the tank and pushes it out the drain.
  2. Close the cold supply and let the tank drain again.
  3. Repeat until the water coming out of the hose runs clear. This may take several cycles on a tank with heavy buildup.

Step 6: Close the drain and refill the tank

  1. Close the drain valve and remove the hose. Check the valve for drips.
  2. Leave the hot water faucet open.
  3. Open the cold water supply valve fully. The tank will begin to fill.
  4. Keep the hot faucet open until water flows from it in a steady stream with no sputtering air. A steady stream means the tank is full and the air is purged.
  5. Close the faucet. Open other hot water faucets briefly to clear air from those lines too.

Step 7: Restore power or gas, only after the tank is full

Electric heaters: never turn the power back on until the tank is completely full of water. Heating elements are designed to be submerged. If you restore power while the tank is empty or partly empty, an exposed element can "dry fire" and burn out within seconds. This is the most common way people ruin an element during a flush. Once a steady stream of water flows from a hot faucet, switch the breaker back on.

If you do burn out an element, replacement elements are available in our water heater elements and conversion kits collection. Match the voltage, wattage and mounting style printed on the old element.

Gas heaters: Turn the gas control from Pilot (or Off) back to On, and set the temperature to your normal setting. If the pilot went out, relight it following the lighting instructions on the heater's label. Plug the heater back in if it has a power vent or electronic control. Check around the drain valve and gas connections, and confirm the burner lights and the flame looks normal.

Recovery takes time: allow about an hour for the tank to reheat fully before you expect normal hot water.

A caution about the T&P relief valve

The temperature and pressure (T&P) relief valve is the safety valve on the top or upper side of the tank, with a discharge pipe running toward the floor. It opens if the tank's temperature or pressure gets dangerously high. It's one of the most important safety devices in your home.

  • Some guides tell you to open the T&P valve to let air in while draining. Opening a hot faucet does the same job and is safer. On an older valve, lifting the lever can leave it unable to reseat, so it keeps dripping afterward.
  • If you test the valve, as many manufacturers recommend doing periodically, stand clear of the discharge pipe. Water released from it is scalding hot. Make sure the discharge pipe is in place and runs to a safe location.
  • If the valve drips or leaks after testing, or if it's discharging on its own, replace it. Frequent discharge can also point to excess pressure in the system, such as a missing or failed thermal expansion tank, which a plumber should check.
  • Never cap, plug or remove the T&P valve or its discharge pipe. A replacement must match the tank's ratings. Browse relief valves and check the BTU/h and pressure ratings on your heater's label before ordering.

Other checks while you're there

  • Anode rod: The anode rod protects the steel tank from corrosion by corroding first. Many manufacturers suggest checking it every few years. If it's worn down to the core wire, replacing it can extend the tank's life. See our dip tubes and anode rods.
  • Leaks and corrosion: Look for rust at the fittings and moisture around the base. Water leaking from the tank itself, rather than from a fitting or valve, usually means the tank needs replacing.

When it's time to replace

If your tank leaks, still rumbles after a thorough flush, or is past its expected service life, a replacement may be the better investment. Browse our residential gas tank water heaters to compare options. If you need help choosing a replacement or finding a part, send us the model and serial number from your heater's label and we'll help you find the right match.
