Radiators that are cold at the top, baseboard that gurgles, a boiler that keeps losing or gaining pressure: these are the most common hot water heating complaints, and most of them come down to air in the system or a pressure problem. This guide shows how to bleed a radiator and baseboard, how to check and restore boiler pressure, and what causes boiler pressure to run too high.

Note: this guide covers hot water (hydronic) systems. Steam radiators work differently: their air vents release air automatically while the system runs, and they should not be bled like a hot water radiator.

Why air gets into a heating system

A hot water heating system is a closed loop, but air still finds its way in:

  • Fresh water carries dissolved air. Every time the system is filled or topped up, new water brings oxygen and other gases that come out of solution as the water heats.
  • Repairs and draining. Replacing a circulator, zone valve or radiator lets air into the piping.
  • Small leaks and low pressure. If pressure at the highest point drops too low, air can be drawn in through vents, valve packing or fittings.
  • Corrosion. Chemical reactions inside steel and iron components can create gas over time.

Air rises to the high points: the top of radiators, the ends of baseboard runs and upper-floor piping. It blocks flow, so the top of a radiator stays cool, and it causes gurgling or "running water" noises. Air also speeds up corrosion and can damage the circulator.

Tools you need

  • Radiator key or screwdriver. Most manual radiator vents have a small square stem that takes a radiator key, such as the Pasco 606 radiator key. Others have a slot for a flat screwdriver or a coin. Keep a spare key with the boiler.
  • A rag and a small cup or bucket to catch water.
  • A garden hose and bucket for purging baseboard zones.
  • A pressure gauge you can trust. If the boiler gauge is stuck or unreadable, a combination temperature and pressure gauge such as the Resideo TD-165 Tridicator or Legend 800-673 is an easy replacement.

How to bleed a radiator, step by step

  1. Turn the heat up first, then off. Run the heat until the radiators are warm so you can find the cold spots. Then set the thermostat down and turn off the circulator (or the boiler) so water is not moving while you bleed. Let the radiators cool enough to touch. Hot water can scald.
  2. Check the boiler pressure. Note the reading on the gauge before you start. You need positive pressure to push the air out.
  3. Start low, work high. A common approach is to begin on the lowest floor and work up, starting with the radiator farthest from the boiler on each floor.
  4. Find the bleed valve. It is a small brass or chrome fitting near the top of the radiator, on the end opposite the supply valve.
  5. Open it slowly. Hold a rag and cup under the vent and turn the key a quarter to half turn counterclockwise. You will hear air hiss. Do not unscrew the stem all the way.
  6. Close it when water comes out. Once a steady stream of water with no sputtering appears, close the vent snugly. Do not overtighten.
  7. Repeat on every radiator that has a vent, then go back to the first one and check again.
  8. Re-check the boiler pressure and top up if needed (see below). Turn the heat back on and confirm the radiators heat evenly.

If a radiator vent is corroded or keeps leaking, replace it. A coin-operated vent such as the Taco 417-3 coin vent (1/8" NPT) is a common upgrade. Match the thread size before ordering.

How to bleed baseboard heat

Most fin-tube baseboard has no bleed valve on each run. Some systems have a small manual vent at the end of a run, under the cover. If yours does, bleed it like a radiator. If not, you remove air by purging each zone through a purge valve near the boiler:

  1. Turn off the boiler and let the water cool.
  2. Find the zone's purge valve. It is usually a boiler drain or a ball valve with a hose thread on the return pipe of each zone, next to a shut-off valve.
  3. Close the zone's shut-off valve between the purge valve and the boiler, so water has to travel through the whole zone before it comes out.
  4. Connect a hose from the purge valve to a bucket or floor drain and open the purge valve.
  5. Feed fresh water in. Lift the fast-fill lever on the boiler fill valve (or open the bypass) so water pushes through the zone. Watch the boiler pressure gauge and do not let it approach the relief valve setting.
  6. Run until the air stops. When the hose runs solid with no bursts of air, close the purge valve, then release the fast-fill lever.
  7. Repeat for each zone, reopen all shut-off valves, set the cold pressure and restart the boiler.

Zones with zone valves may need the valve opened manually during purging. Check the manual lever on the zone valve or see our zone valve guide.

Stop bleeding by hand: automatic air vents

Automatic air vents release air on their own at the system's high points, at air separators and on air scoops. A small float inside opens the vent when air collects and closes it when water returns.

  • Taco 418-4 Hy-Vent (1/2" x 3/4" NPT) and Taco 400-4 Hy-Vent (1/8" NPT) for high points and air scoops.
  • Caleffi MAXCAL 501502A (3/4" NPT female), a larger-capacity vent.
  • Caleffi Robocal 502710A (1/8" male, with check valve), a compact vent for manifolds and terminal units. The check valve lets you remove it without draining the system.
  • Resideo SuperVent SV175 (1/2", with check valve).

For systems with constant air problems, an air separator near the boiler removes air far better than a scoop. Browse air separators and all air vents.

Checking and restoring boiler pressure

The pressure gauge on the boiler (often combined with a thermometer) shows the pressure of the heating loop. Read it with the system cold and again when it is hot.

  • Cold: many residential systems are filled to about 12 to 15 psi. That is enough to lift water to the top of a typical two-story home with a few psi to spare at the highest radiator.
  • Hot: pressure rises as the water expands. Readings of roughly 18 to 25 psi are common in a hot residential system.
  • Relief valve: most residential boilers have a relief valve set at 30 psi.

These are general figures. Your boiler manual gives the correct range for your system, and taller homes need a higher fill pressure.

How to top up the pressure

After bleeding, pressure usually drops. Most systems refill through a boiler fill valve (also called a feed valve or pressure reducing valve) on the cold water line:

  • On an automatic fill valve such as the Taco 329-3, Resideo FM911 or Caleffi 573012A COMBO AutoFill, make sure the inlet valve is open. The valve should bring the system up to its set pressure on its own.
  • If the system is still low, lift the fast-fill lever briefly while watching the gauge, then release it.
  • Many combi boilers have a built-in fill valve or filling loop. Follow the manual. See our combi boiler guide for more on combi maintenance.

If you have to top up often, there is a leak somewhere: at a radiator valve, a fitting, a relief valve that drips, or inside the boiler. Find and fix it, because constant fresh water brings in more air and minerals.

Boiler pressure too high? Common causes

If the gauge climbs well above the normal hot range, or approaches 30 psi, look at these causes in order:

1. Failed or waterlogged expansion tank

The expansion tank gives heated water room to expand. Inside, a diaphragm or bladder separates the system water from a cushion of air. When the air charge leaks away or the bladder fails, the tank fills with water and can no longer absorb expansion, so pressure spikes every time the boiler fires.

  • Quick checks: tap the tank. A good tank sounds hollow at the top. Press the Schrader (tire) valve briefly: water coming out means the bladder has failed.
  • Pre-charge: the air charge should be checked with the tank isolated from system pressure and is usually set to match the cold fill pressure. Follow the tank manufacturer's instructions.
  • Replacement: heating tanks such as the Amtrol EX-15 and EX-30 Extrol are common in homes. Size by system water volume. See all heating expansion tanks, and read our guide Expansion Tanks: What They Do and What Size You Need.

Older systems may use a steel compression tank without a bladder. These slowly waterlog and need to be drained to restore the air cushion.

2. Leaking fill valve (pressure reducing valve)

If pressure creeps up even when the boiler is cold or off, the fill valve may be passing water from the higher-pressure domestic supply. Close the valve on the cold water feed for a day. If the creep stops, the fill valve is the culprit. Some valves can be rebuilt (Caleffi offers an AutoFill replacement cartridge); otherwise replace the valve. Browse boiler fill and feed valves.

3. Overfilling

Holding the fast-fill lever too long, or setting the fill valve too high, leaves the system with too much cold pressure. Drain a little water from a boiler drain with the system cold until you reach the correct cold pressure.

4. A leaking indirect water heater coil

If you have an indirect water heater, a leak in its internal coil can push domestic water (at street pressure) into the boiler loop. If pressure keeps rising and the fill valve is shut, have a professional test the coil.

When the relief valve discharges, call a pro

The boiler relief valve is a safety device. If it releases water, the system reached its set pressure (usually 30 psi) or the valve itself has failed. Do not plug, cap or remove the discharge pipe, and never replace a relief valve with one rated higher than the boiler allows.

A relief valve that opens is a warning sign. Turn the boiler off and have a licensed heating professional find the cause. Old relief valves can also leak from mineral buildup. A professional can replace one with the correct pressure rating and capacity, such as the Watts 0274428 (3/4", 30 psi). See all relief valves.

Shop the parts

  • Air vents and radiator vents
  • Air separators
  • Boiler fill valves and feed valves
  • Heating expansion tanks
  • Relief valves
  • Temperature and pressure gauges
  • Pressure gauges
  • Radiator valves

Frequently asked questions

How do I know if my radiator needs bleeding?

The top of the radiator is cool while the bottom is warm, or you hear gurgling. A radiator that is cold all over usually has a different problem, such as a closed valve, a stuck zone valve or no flow.

Should the heating be on or off when bleeding radiators?

Run it first to find the cold radiators, then turn it off and let the system cool before opening any vent. This reduces the risk of burns and lets air settle at the top.

What should my boiler pressure be?

Many residential systems run about 12 to 15 psi cold and roughly 18 to 25 psi hot, with a 30 psi relief valve. Your boiler manual has the correct range for your home.

Why does my boiler pressure go up when the heat is on?

Some rise is normal because water expands as it heats. A large jump, especially toward 30 psi, usually means the expansion tank has lost its air charge or failed.

Why does my boiler keep losing pressure?

Bleeding releases a little pressure, which is normal. Ongoing loss means a leak or a relief valve that drips. Check radiator valves, fittings and the relief valve discharge pipe.

Many home plumbing projects mix old and new: an existing copper system with a new run of PEX for a bathroom remodel, a basement finish or a repair. Connecting PEX to copper is straightforward once you pick the right transition fitting. There are three common methods: sweat (solder) adapters, push-to-connect fittings, and crimp or expansion adapters that join to the copper by solder, press or thread.

This guide explains how each method works, when to use it, and the mistakes to avoid.

Before you start: know your pipe sizes

Most residential copper and PEX in the US uses copper tube size (CTS), so 1/2" PEX matches 1/2" copper tube and 3/4" matches 3/4". Even so, confirm what you have:

  • Copper: Type M, L or K copper all share the same outside diameter for a given nominal size. A 1/2" copper tube measures about 5/8" outside diameter, and 3/4" measures about 7/8".
  • PEX: Check the print line on the tubing for its size, type (PEX-A, B or C), and the fitting standards it's listed for, such as ASTM F1807, F2159 or F1960.

Not sure which PEX you have? Our guide to PEX-A vs PEX-B explains the differences and the matching fitting systems.

Safety and preparation

  • Shut off the water at the main valve or the nearest fixture valve, open a faucet below the work area to drain the line, and keep a bucket and towels handy.
  • Soldering uses an open flame. Wear safety glasses, keep a fire extinguisher nearby, protect nearby framing with a heat shield, and check the area for smoldering after you finish. Use lead-free solder and flux rated for potable water.
  • Electrical bonding: In many homes, metal water piping is part of the electrical grounding or bonding system. Replacing a section of copper with PEX can interrupt that path. If you cut into a copper line, especially near the water meter or main shut-off, have an electrician check whether a bonding jumper is needed.
  • Water heaters: Many PEX manufacturers and local codes don't allow PEX to connect directly to a gas water heater. Use metal pipe or approved connectors for a minimum distance (often 18 inches) from the heater, and follow the tubing manufacturer's instructions.

Method 1: Sweat (solder) adapters

A sweat adapter has a copper socket or spigot on one end and a PEX barb on the other. You solder the copper end onto the existing copper pipe, then attach the PEX with a crimp, clamp or expansion connection. Common versions include female sweat x PEX and male sweat (fitting) x PEX adapters.

How to do it

  1. Cut and prepare the copper. Cut the copper square with a tubing cutter. Deburr the inside and outside, then clean the pipe end and the fitting socket with emery cloth or a fitting brush until shiny.
  2. Solder the adapter before attaching the PEX. Apply flux, assemble, heat the fitting evenly, and feed solder into the joint. Let the joint cool completely. Never heat a fitting with PEX already attached, because the flame or conducted heat will damage the tubing.
  3. Attach the PEX. Once the adapter is cool, cut the PEX square, slide on a crimp or clamp ring, push the PEX fully onto the barb, and make the connection with the correct tool. Check crimp rings with a go/no-go gauge.
  4. Test. Turn the water back on slowly and check every joint for leaks.

Tip: If you can, solder the adapter onto a short piece of copper first (on a workbench), then connect that assembly to the existing pipe with a coupling. This keeps flame work away from walls and lets the joint cool before you work near the PEX.

Best for: Permanent, concealed connections where you're comfortable soldering. Sweat joints are proven and inexpensive. Find fittings and couplings in our copper sweat fittings collection.

Method 2: Push-to-connect fittings

Push-to-connect fittings (such as SharkBite and similar brands) join copper, PEX and CPVC without solder or crimp tools. Inside the fitting, a stainless steel grip ring holds the pipe, and an O-ring seals it. A push-to-connect coupling can join 1/2" copper directly to 1/2" PEX.

How to do it

  1. Cut both pipes square with a tubing cutter (copper) and a PEX cutter (PEX).
  2. Deburr and clean the copper. A sharp edge or burr can cut the O-ring. Remove any burrs and wipe the pipe clean. The pipe surface must be smooth and free of scratches or flattening where the O-ring seals.
  3. Check for a PEX stiffener. PEX needs a tube support (stiffener) inside the pipe end. Many brass push fittings include one already installed. If yours doesn't, insert one according to the fitting instructions.
  4. Mark the insertion depth on each pipe, using the depth gauge or the fitting's instructions.
  5. Push each pipe in firmly until it reaches the mark. Turn the water on and check for leaks.

Best for: Quick repairs, tight spaces where a torch isn't safe, and anyone without soldering or crimping tools. Many push fittings can be removed with a release clip or tool and reused, depending on the manufacturer. Check the fitting's listing and local code before burying one in a wall or using it underground. Shop push fittings.

Method 3: Crimp or expansion adapters (with threaded or press options)

If you already have PEX tools, you can use a transition adapter made for your PEX system and connect it to the copper side in whatever way suits the job.

Crimp and clamp adapters (F1807 / F2159)

These have a PEX insert barb for crimp or clamp rings on one end and a copper connection on the other: a sweat end, a male or female thread, or a press end. They work with PEX-B, PEX-C, and PEX-A tubing that's listed for crimp or clamp connections. Browse PEX crimp fittings (F1807) for sweat and threaded adapters.

Expansion adapters (F1960)

For PEX-A expansion systems, adapters come with an expansion fitting on the PEX end and a copper sweat or thread on the other. Make the copper side first (solder and cool, if sweating), then expand the PEX-A tubing and ring and push it onto the adapter. Allow the joint to shrink fully before pressurizing it.

Threaded transitions

A threaded transition avoids soldering near the PEX: solder a female or male threaded adapter onto the copper, then thread on a matching PEX adapter. Use thread sealant tape or pipe dope rated for potable water, and don't overtighten. Threaded joints also make it easy to disconnect later.

Press transitions

If you have a copper press tool, you can press a fitting onto the copper and use a press x PEX adapter, which avoids an open flame entirely. Use fittings and jaws from the same press system.

You'll need the right cutter and crimp, clamp or expansion tool for the PEX side. See our PEX tools.

Which method should you use?

Method Tools needed Pros Watch out for
Sweat adapter Torch, solder, flux, plus PEX crimp/clamp/expansion tool Permanent, proven, low fitting cost Open flame; heat damage to PEX if soldered with tubing attached
Push-to-connect Cutters and deburr tool Fast, no flame, often removable Higher fitting cost; pipe must be clean and undamaged; check code for concealed use
Crimp/expansion adapter (sweat, thread or press) PEX tool, plus torch, wrenches or press tool Matches your existing PEX system; flexible options Use rings and fittings listed for your PEX type

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Soldering with PEX attached. Always solder first and let the joint cool.
  • Skipping deburring. Burrs on copper can cut O-rings in push fittings and cause leaks.
  • Mixing fitting systems. Don't use F1960 expansion fittings on PEX-B, or crimp rings from one system with fittings that aren't listed for them.
  • Not supporting the transition. Secure both the copper and PEX near the fitting so the joint doesn't carry the weight or movement of the pipe.
  • Forgetting the bonding jumper when replacing copper that's part of the electrical bonding path.

If you're unsure about soldering, gas water heater connections or electrical bonding, hire a licensed plumber. For help matching adapters to your pipe, send us your pipe size and PEX type and we'll help you find the right fittings.

Walk into any plumbing aisle and you'll see PEX labeled as PEX-A, PEX-B or PEX-C. All three are cross-linked polyethylene tubing, and all three are used for hot and cold water supply lines in homes across the US. The letters refer to how the tubing is cross-linked, and that difference affects how flexible the pipe is, which fittings and tools it works with, how it handles a kink, and what it costs.

This guide focuses on the two types you'll see most often, PEX-A and PEX-B, so you can pick the right pipe and connection system for your project.

What "cross-linked" means

Polyethylene on its own softens with heat and isn't strong enough for pressurized hot water. Cross-linking creates chemical bonds between the long polyethylene molecules, turning them into a three-dimensional network. That network gives PEX its resistance to heat, pressure and creep, while keeping it flexible.

The ASTM F876 standard requires a specified range of cross-linking for PEX tubing, whatever the method. So PEX-A, PEX-B and PEX-C are all "real" PEX that meets the same basic standard. In the US, PEX tubing that meets ASTM F876 and F877 typically carries the same standard pressure ratings: 160 psi at 73°F, 100 psi at 180°F and 80 psi at 200°F. Check the print line on the tubing for its exact ratings and listings.

How PEX-A is made: the Engel (peroxide) method

PEX-A is cross-linked using the Engel method, also called the peroxide method. Peroxide is mixed into the polyethylene, and cross-linking happens while the material is hot, during or right after extrusion. Because it occurs while the polymer is still in a molten state, PEX-A typically reaches the highest degree of cross-linking of the three types, often cited at around 85%.

The result is a pipe that's noticeably softer and more flexible, with a strong "thermal memory": when heated, it tries to return to its original shape. That property is the basis of cold-expansion fittings and heat-gun kink repair, covered below.

How PEX-B is made: the silane (moisture-cure) method

PEX-B uses the silane method. A silane compound is grafted onto the polyethylene, the tubing is extruded, and cross-linking happens afterward when the pipe is exposed to heat and moisture (for example in a steam or hot water bath). PEX-B typically reaches a cross-linking level of around 65% to 70%.

PEX-B is stiffer than PEX-A and has less thermal memory. It's widely used for residential water lines and is common in big-box retail.

What about PEX-C? PEX-C is cross-linked after extrusion by electron-beam radiation. It sits between A and B in flexibility for many products, and it's usually joined with crimp or clamp fittings.

Flexibility and handling

  • PEX-A is the most flexible. It makes tighter bends with fewer fittings and uncoils more easily, which helps in cold weather and in tight framing. A tighter bend radius means fewer elbows and fewer connections that could leak.
  • PEX-B is stiffer and has more coil memory, so it tends to spring back toward its coiled shape. It needs a larger bend radius, and bend supports or 90° fittings are used more often. Some installers like that stiffness for long, straight runs that look neater.

Always follow the tubing manufacturer's minimum bend radius. Bending tighter than allowed can kink the pipe.

Fittings: expansion vs crimp and clamp

The fitting system is the most practical difference between PEX-A and PEX-B, because it determines which tools you need.

Connection Standard How it works Typical tubing
Cold expansion with PEX ring ASTM F1960 An expansion tool stretches the pipe end and a PEX ring. The fitting is inserted, and the pipe shrinks back around it. PEX-A
Copper crimp ring ASTM F1807 (metal insert) / F2159 (plastic insert) An insert fitting goes into the pipe, and a copper ring is compressed with a crimp tool. PEX-B, PEX-C, and many PEX-A tubes
Stainless steel clamp (cinch) ring ASTM F1807 / F2159 fittings with F2098 rings A stainless band is cinched over an insert fitting with a ratcheting clamp tool. PEX-B, PEX-C, and many PEX-A tubes
Push-to-connect ASSE 1061 The pipe pushes into a fitting with an internal grip ring and O-ring. No tool needed beyond a cutter and deburr tool. All types listed by the fitting maker

Expansion (F1960) fittings

Expansion fittings rely on PEX-A's thermal memory. After the pipe is expanded over the fitting, it shrinks back and grips tightly. Expansion joints are popular with professionals because the pipe is expanded rather than squeezed, so the fitting's inside diameter can be larger than a crimp fitting of the same size, which means less flow restriction. A joint made in cold weather takes longer to shrink down, so give it time before pressure testing.

Standard F1960 expansion fittings are generally intended for PEX-A only. PEX-B doesn't have enough memory to shrink reliably around them. A few manufacturers offer their own expansion systems for PEX-B, but those use specific rings and fittings from that maker. Never mix systems unless the manufacturer lists them as compatible.

Crimp and clamp fittings

Crimp and clamp fittings work on PEX-B and PEX-C, and many PEX-A tubes are also listed for them. Check the print line on your tubing for the ASTM standards it's listed with. Crimp tools must be sized and calibrated for the ring, and every connection should be checked with a go/no-go gauge. Clamp (cinch) tools usually cover several sizes with one tool and release automatically when the clamp is complete.

Shop insert fittings in our PEX crimp fittings (F1807) collection, or browse the full range of PEX fittings.

Cost

Prices change, but some general patterns hold:

  • Tubing: PEX-B is usually less expensive per foot than PEX-A.
  • Tools: Crimp and clamp tools generally cost much less than a PEX expansion tool, especially a battery-powered one. For a small DIY repair, the tool cost often decides the choice.
  • Labor and fittings: For a whole-house repipe, PEX-A's flexibility can reduce the number of fittings and speed up installation, which offsets some of the material cost for professionals.

See our PEX tools for cutters, crimpers, clamp tools and expansion tools.

Kink repair

Kinks happen, especially when you uncoil tubing in a hurry. Here PEX-A has a real advantage:

  • PEX-A: Many PEX-A manufacturers allow kinked tubing to be repaired with a heat gun. Warm the kinked section evenly, and the pipe's thermal memory returns it to its original round shape. Follow the manufacturer's procedure. Never use an open flame, and don't overheat the pipe.
  • PEX-B: A kink in PEX-B generally can't be heat-repaired. Cut out the damaged section and install a coupling.

Other considerations

  • UV exposure: All PEX is damaged by sunlight. Store it out of the sun, and follow the manufacturer's maximum UV exposure time. Don't install it where it's exposed to sunlight.
  • Heat sources: Keep PEX away from flue pipes, recessed lights and other high-heat sources. Many manufacturers and codes require a metal connector or a minimum distance (often 18 inches) at a gas water heater's connections.
  • Freeze tolerance: PEX is more forgiving than rigid pipe when water freezes, but it can still split. Insulate or protect lines in unheated spaces.
  • Codes: PEX is accepted by the major US plumbing codes, but local rules vary. Check with your local building department.

PEX-A vs PEX-B: quick comparison

PEX-A PEX-B
Cross-linking method Engel (peroxide), during extrusion Silane (moisture cure), after extrusion
Typical cross-link level About 85% About 65–70%
Flexibility Most flexible, tight bends Stiffer, more coil memory
Main fitting system F1960 expansion (also crimp/clamp if listed) Crimp or clamp (F1807 / F2159)
Kink repair Heat gun, per manufacturer Cut out and couple
Typical cost Higher tubing and tool cost Lower tubing and tool cost

Which should you choose?

  • Choose PEX-A if you're doing a larger project or repipe, want the most flexible tubing, prefer expansion fittings with less flow restriction, or want the option of heat-repairing kinks.
  • Choose PEX-B if you're making repairs or a smaller project, want lower tubing and tool cost, or already own a crimp or clamp tool.
  • Either way: Use one connection system consistently, with tubing, fittings and rings that are listed together, and pressure test before closing up walls.

Browse PEX pipe and tubing in both types, in a range of sizes and colors. Need help matching tubing to fittings? Send us the print line from your existing pipe and we'll help you find compatible parts.

When one room in a hydronic (hot water) heating system goes cold, or one zone won't shut off, the zone valve is often the culprit. The good news is that many zone valve failures are in the power head (actuator), not the valve body, so the repair can be simpler than it looks. This guide explains how zone valves work, how to tell 2-wire, 3-wire and end-switch valves apart, and how the two most common residential brands, Taco and Honeywell (Resideo), compare. It also covers the general replacement steps.

How a zone valve works

A zone valve is an electrically operated valve on the supply or return pipe of one heating zone. When the thermostat for that zone calls for heat, it sends low voltage (usually 24 VAC from a transformer) to the valve's actuator. The valve opens, hot water flows through that zone's baseboard, radiators or radiant tubing, and the room warms up. When the thermostat is satisfied, the valve closes again.

Most residential zone valves have two parts:

  • The valve body: The brass part piped into the system with sweat (solder), threaded (NPT), flare or press connections.
  • The power head or actuator: The electrical part that opens and closes the valve. On most Taco and Honeywell residential valves, you can replace the head without draining the system or cutting pipe.

Heat motor vs motorized actuators

The two brands use different ways to move the valve:

  • Taco 570 series (heat motor): The head contains a wax-filled element wrapped with a small heater. When 24 VAC is applied, the heater warms the wax, which expands and pushes the valve open. Heat motor valves open gradually, so a short delay after the thermostat calls is normal.
  • Honeywell V8043 / V8044 (motorized, spring return): A small electric motor drives the valve open, and a spring closes it when power is removed. Honeywell lists about 30 seconds of valve timing on the V8044A.

2-wire vs 3-wire vs end switch

Wiring is where most replacement mistakes happen, so identify your valve's wiring before you order parts.

  • 2-wire (no end switch): The thermostat circuit powers the actuator, and that's it. The valve doesn't send any signal back to the boiler or circulator. These valves are used where a zone control panel or another device handles boiler and pump control.
  • End switch valves: An end switch is a small switch inside the head that closes when the valve is fully open. It is typically wired to start the boiler or circulator, so the pump only runs once a zone is actually open. This is the most common setup in residential systems that don't use a zone control panel.
    • 3-wire: Some end switch valves share one terminal between the actuator and the end switch. Taco's 570 series uses a three-terminal block.
    • 4-wire: Others keep the end switch completely separate. A Honeywell V8043E, for example, has motor leads plus separate end switch leads.
  • Terminal block vs lead wires: Some heads have screw terminals, and others come with pre-attached lead wires. Honeywell's V8043F, for example, uses a terminal block, while the V8043E has 18" lead wires.

Tip: Before you disconnect anything, take a clear photo of the existing wiring and write down the full model number printed on the head and on the valve body.

Common Taco zone valve models

Taco 570 series (Gold Series heat motor valves)

The 570 family (570, 571, 572 and 573) covers different pipe sizes. It is one of the most widely installed residential zone valve lines in the US. The Taco 571-2 is a 3/4" sweat, 2-way, normally closed heat motor valve with an end switch and a 3-wire terminal block. It is the model people search for most when they replace a Taco zone valve on 3/4" copper.

If the valve body is fine and only the head has failed, the Taco 555-050RP replacement power head fits 570 series valves. It lets you service the valve without removing the body from the pipe.

Taco Zone Sentry

Zone Sentry is a separate Taco line. It is a motorized ball valve design (model numbers such as Z075C2 for 3/4" sweat), available in 2-way and 3-way versions with an end switch. It has a manual override on top that also shows the valve position. Zone Sentry heads aren't interchangeable with 570 series heads, so match the replacement to the line you have.

Common Honeywell (Resideo) zone valve models

Honeywell Home zone valves are now made by Resideo, so you may see either name on the label and packaging.

  • V8043 (2-way, 24 VAC): The most common Honeywell residential zone valve.
    • V8043A (normally closed) and V8043B (normally open) are the basic versions.
    • V8043E adds an end switch with 18" lead wires.
    • V8043F adds an end switch with a terminal block.
    A popular choice for 3/4" copper is the Honeywell V8043E1012: 3/4" sweat, normally closed, with 18" leads.
  • V8044 (3-way diverting, 24 VAC): Used where flow has to be diverted between two paths instead of simply turned on and off.
  • V4043 / V4044: The 120 VAC (line-voltage) versions of the V8043 and V8044. Never install a 24 VAC head on a 120 VAC circuit, or the reverse.
  • 1000 series (V8043C/D/F/G): Newer valve bodies that use their own replacement actuators. Match the actuator part number to the valve letter.

Taco vs Honeywell: how they compare

Taco 570 series Honeywell V8043
Actuator type Heat motor (wax element) Electric motor with spring return
Opening speed Gradual Faster
Typical voltage 24 VAC 24 VAC (V8043); 120 VAC (V4043)
Wiring 3-wire terminal block with end switch Lead wire or terminal block; with or without end switch, depending on letter
Head replaceable without draining Yes (555-050RP for 570 series) Yes, on most models (with a matching replacement head or actuator)

Neither brand is "better" across the board. In most cases, the right answer is to replace like with like, so the wiring, controls and pipe connections stay the same. If you switch brands, you'll usually need to replace the whole valve and confirm the new valve's wiring works with your thermostat, transformer and boiler or zone control.

Power head or full valve: which do you need?

Replace only the power head if:

  • The valve won't open (zone stays cold) or won't close (zone overheats), and the body isn't leaking.
  • Your controls show 24 VAC at the head during a call for heat, but nothing happens. On a motorized valve, there's no motor movement. On a heat motor valve, the head doesn't open after a reasonable delay.
  • The manual lever moves freely, which usually means the valve body isn't seized.

Replace the full valve if:

  • The body or stem is leaking.
  • The valve is stuck open or closed even with a working head, for example because of debris or a worn seat.
  • You're changing brands, pipe size or connection type, or the original head is no longer available.

Browse heads and actuators for both brands in our zone valve replacement heads collection.

General replacement steps

Safety first: Zone valves connect to your boiler's electrical and control circuits, and full valve replacement means working on a pressurized hot water system. Turn off power to the boiler and zone controls before you touch any wiring. Always hire a licensed HVAC or hydronic professional for any work on gas appliances, line-voltage (120V) wiring, soldering, or draining and refilling a boiler system. If you're unsure, stop and call a pro.

Replacing a power head (low-voltage, no draining)

  1. Turn off power to the boiler and to the zone control or transformer.
  2. Photograph the wiring and label each wire.
  3. Disconnect the wires from the terminals or wire nuts.
  4. Remove the head from the valve body, following the manufacturer's instructions for your model.
  5. Fit the new head and make sure it seats fully on the valve body.
  6. Reconnect the wires exactly as before, following the wiring diagram supplied with the new head.
  7. Restore power, raise the zone thermostat, and confirm the valve opens, the end switch starts the boiler or circulator (if used), and the zone heats up.

Replacing the full valve

This job involves isolating or draining the zone, cutting out the old valve, and installing the new body (soldering, threading or press fitting). After that, you refill, purge air and check for leaks. Leave this to a licensed professional unless you're experienced with hydronic systems.

Before you order

  • Copy the full model number from the head and the valve body.
  • Confirm the voltage (24 VAC vs 120 VAC), normally open vs normally closed, and whether you need an end switch.
  • Confirm the pipe size and connection type (sweat, NPT, flare or press) if you're replacing the full valve.
